stories.topic: Pushpesh Pant's Maps of Souring Agents
stories.summary: Opening the episode, Amit recalls his Seen and the Unseen conversation with food writer Pushpesh Pant. Pant said he carries imagined maps in his head that have nothing to do with political boundaries. One is drawn by which souring agent a region cooks with: tamarind or kokum, and so on.
stories.insight: Political borders are only one way to divide a landscape, and often not the most meaningful one. Food, language and ecology draw their own lines, and those lines follow how people actually live.
stories.quote: he said that in his mind there are all kinds of imagined maps which are based, for example, on what souring agent you use for your food

stories.topic: Aanchal Malhotra and the Rant That Stopped Mid-Sentence
stories.summary: While researching her book on Partition, Aanchal Malhotra sat with a Pakistani family that had lived through it. One family member began ranting that Hindus are this and Hindus are that, then suddenly remembered that Aanchal was sitting right there. The woman turned to her and reassured her that she wasn't included.
stories.insight: Prejudice survives on abstractions such as 'Hindus', 'foreigners' and the nation. It struggles when the abstraction becomes a real person sitting across the table. Amit's lesson is that the concrete human connection is real and the line on the map is the fiction.
stories.quote: And that made me think about the distinction between the abstract and the concrete. The line on the map is abstract.

stories.topic: The Border Town 300 Metres From Mexico
stories.summary: The idea for this episode came alive for Ajay while he was reading human stories about the Texas–Mexico border. One interviewee lived in a border town with a Mexican city 300 metres away. They said the people across the line were their friends and neighbours. To them, the national debate about two countries and keeping migrants out felt like something that belonged to people far away.
stories.insight: The nation is an imagined community that is strongest far from the border. Up close, life follows the gravity law: your people are simply the people near you.
stories.quote: Whereas the reality is the bloke that I meet when I wake up in the morning and who do I have chai with?

stories.topic: Border Haats: Rupees Only, Then Barter
stories.summary: India has built eight border haats on the India–Bangladesh border, which Ajay calls pitifully few for a border that long. These are controlled marketplaces where people from both sides meet to trade. The rule was that all transactions must be in Indian rupees. The other side pointed out that they had no rupees, so the rule was relaxed to allow barter. Ajay also mentions the free movement zone on the Burma border near Nagaland and the easy India–Nepal border.
stories.insight: The urge to trade keeps finding ways around bureaucratic rules. Ajay calls these half-open arrangements a healthy step away from a 'Stalinist' total cutoff and wants them amplified, because both countries gain from trade.
stories.quote: all transactions shall only be conducted in the Indian rupee. Okay, but then those guys say, but we don't have Indian rupees. Okay, fine, we'll accept barter.

stories.topic: Two Lahores at Three in the Morning
stories.summary: In 2006 Amit spent a few weeks travelling through Pakistan to follow an Indian cricket tour, live-blogging as he went. At 3 AM in Lahore he posted a photo of kids playing cricket in the street. Food could be ordered from anywhere, and despite the Islamic Republic, alcohol and recreational drugs were easy to get. Apart from one or two stray incidents, he met warmth everywhere. He saw two layers sitting uneasily together: the effusive Punjabiyat of kite-flying festivals that Indians know well, and the shrill harshness of the Islamic Republic state. He also notes that well into the 1950s the India–Pakistan border was porous, and people crossed freely to visit relatives.
stories.insight: A society's lived culture and its state ideology are separate layers, and the culture often has far more in common with the supposed enemy than the state admits. The closed border we take for granted today is a recent normal.
stories.quote: I found this sort of interesting overlapping Pakistans over there, overlapping Lahores as it were.

stories.topic: Learning English by Copying Agota Kristof
stories.summary: A participant in Amit's writing course told him that Hindi was her first language, she was only now learning English, and asked what she should do. Amit pointed her to Agota Kristof, who learned French as an adult and wrote in pared-down prose. She later told him she had sat with the Notebook Trilogy and copied its sentences out herself.
stories.insight: Copying a stylist's sentences is an old way to absorb how a language moves. Spare prose by someone who also came to the language late is an especially good model for a learner.
stories.quote: to sort of get the rhythm of the language, get a feel of the language, internalize it.

recommendations.item: Pushpesh Pant Feasts on the Buffet of Life (Episode 326 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's first example of maps that ignore political lines, at the very start of the episode.
recommendations.reason: This is where Pant describes the imagined maps in his head, such as maps drawn by which souring agent a region cooks with. It is a delightful alternative way to see geography.

recommendations.item: Arati Kumar-Rao Took a One-Way Ticket (Episode 383 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit refers to this recent episode in his introduction (the transcript is broken here) and links it in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: It looks at people's lived connection with the land they inhabit, which sits in contrast to the political maps taught in geography class.

recommendations.item: Marginlands: Indian Landscapes on the Brink
recommendations.creator: Arati Kumar-Rao
recommendations.context: Listed in the show notes alongside Amit's episode with the author.
recommendations.reason: It is a companion to the lived, land-based way of seeing geography that Amit holds up against lines on maps.

recommendations.creator: Saadat Hasan Manto
recommendations.context: Amit's mid-episode 'pointer', right after Ajay's account of life on the border.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great short story about one of the most tragic borders, and one that is close to home.

recommendations.item: Memories and Things (Episode 195 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with Aanchal Malhotra, the source of the Lahore story about the rant that stopped mid-sentence.
recommendations.reason: This is where Amit first started thinking seriously about abstract categories versus concrete human connection.

recommendations.creator: Aanchal Malhotra
recommendations.context: Amit mentions it as he tells the story from her research.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great book on Partition, built from the memories of families who lived through it.

recommendations.item: A Trade Deficit With a Babysitter
recommendations.creator: Tim Harford
recommendations.context: Amit cites it when arguing that worry over trade deficits is misplaced nationalist rhetoric.
recommendations.reason: Harford keeps paying his babysitter and she never pays him back, so he runs a 'deficit' with her that is plainly good for both of them. It is a neat demolition of trade-deficit panic.

recommendations.creator: WEH Lecky
recommendations.context: Amit introduces Lecky's 'expanding circle' as a moral framework he thinks about a lot.
recommendations.reason: It is the source of the idea that the circle of people we grant moral consideration widens over history, from family to tribe to nation, and is destined to include all of humanity.

recommendations.creator: Peter Singer
recommendations.context: Mentioned as Singer's extension of Lecky's thesis.
recommendations.reason: Singer argued that the circle will expand beyond humans to include animals.

recommendations.creator: Kevin Kelly
recommendations.context: Amit invokes it while explaining how the internet freed him from communities of circumstance.
recommendations.reason: A creator doesn't need a mass audience, only a thousand true fans. Once geography stops mattering, those fans can be scattered anywhere in the world and still make the work viable.

recommendations.creator: Florian Henckel von Donnersmarck
recommendations.context: Amit's mid-episode recommendation after the discussion of East and West Germany.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a masterpiece and possibly one of the finest debut films he has seen. It brings out the full tragedy of what Germany's separation did to people.

recommendations.item: Jhumpa Lahiri on Writing, Translation, and Crossing Between Cultures (Episode 17 of Conversations With Tyler)
recommendations.creator: Tyler Cowen
recommendations.context: This is how Amit discovered Agota Kristof.
recommendations.reason: Lahiri had learned Italian from scratch as an adult and written a book in it. When Tyler Cowen asked her about her models, she named Agota Kristof.

recommendations.creator: Agota Kristof
recommendations.reason: Kristof was a Hungarian writer who fled during the twentieth century, learned French as an adult and wrote these books in it. Late-arriving writers like Nabokov can revel in florid language, but Kristof stripped both prose and narrative to the bone, with enormous power. It is set in a constantly shifting borderland during an unnamed war, with children trying to make sense of the world, so it fits the episode's theme too.

core_ideas.concept: The Gravity Model of Human Interaction
core_ideas.explanation: Economists found that trade between two countries is roughly proportional to the product of their GDPs divided by the square of the distance between them, which mirrors Newton's law of gravitation. 'Distance' has to be read broadly: two English-speaking countries are effectively closer than an anglophone and a francophone one. Ajay generalises the model to all human interaction. Double the distance and interaction falls by four times, not two. This is the logic behind dense cities, and he suggests that even the length of a lift ride between floors changes how often neighbours meet.
core_ideas.quote: That what people do with each other is inversely proportional to the distance squared.

core_ideas.concept: Borders Hurt Most the People Who Live On Them
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's thought experiment is to zoom into a border such as the one between West Bengal and Bangladesh. There is no demilitarised zone, just a field with a house on each side. The families talk, party, marry, trade and send their kids to play together. Draw a hard line through that and a person at the centre of the circle loses half their social network. Fifty or sixty kilometres away, the border barely matters. The cost of a border falls hardest on exactly the people who are each other's closest circle.
core_ideas.quote: So you've taken the smallest unit of that tribe and you've put a line through their heart

core_ideas.explanation: Lines on maps, nationalism and ideas of purity are abstractions. People eating, drinking, marrying and being friends with each other is the concrete reality. Amit worries that the smartphone age keeps us lost in toxic abstractions that blind us to how much we already share, a shared culture he describes as a khichdi of food and dress.
core_ideas.quote: We are together on the dinner table when we have Biryani and Raita.

core_ideas.explanation: Borders behave like fractals: the closer you look, the longer they get, so fencing and patrolling them properly is close to impossible. The incentive to trade forest honey for rice is strong, fences get wire-cut, and walls can be climbed or blown open. Ajay argues that sealing efforts, including Trump's wall, are largely political posturing. In practice India's borders with Nepal and Bangladesh are open, and he considers that a decent state of affairs.
core_ideas.quote: Realistically, it is not possible to seal off the border.

core_ideas.concept: The European Union as a Civilising Project
core_ideas.explanation: Europe was the champion of nationalist cruelty: Germany invaded France in 1870, 1914 and 1940, and millions died. From the ashes of the Second World War came the EU. Today people drive across the French–German border with no papers and no checkpoints and work freely on the other side, as full participants rather than immigrants. Ajay sees this as the height of civilisation. The state keeps its legitimate job, such as protecting people from violence, but stays out of their natural dealings with each other. Amit sums it up as society coming first and the state being subsidiary.
core_ideas.quote: And that to me is the height of civilization. Saying, yeah, you have your nation state, but don't interfere in the lives of the people.

core_ideas.explanation: Open borders produce blended cultures where people speak each other's languages. Ajay points to the hybrid Gujarati–Marathi culture on the Gujarat–Maharashtra border and the Marathi–Kannada culture on the Maharashtra–Karnataka border. At the French–German border the culture is neither French nor German but a mix of both. People at an edge identify with their neighbours, not with a distant capital.
core_ideas.quote: So at the French German border there is actually neither French nor German culture. There is a hybrid French German culture. What they identify with is each other.

core_ideas.explanation: Fiscal deficits deserve worry; bilateral trade deficits do not. A trade deficit with China just means Indians bought more from Chinese people than the reverse, and every voluntary trade benefits both sides. Thinking about trade in terms of nation states is nationalist framing. If Amit wants to trade with someone in Canada or in Pune, it should be nobody's business.
core_ideas.quote: Because countries do not trade with each other. People trade with people.

core_ideas.explanation: Globally, the gravity model predicts trade between countries reasonably well. Its biggest misses are in South Asia, where it predicts far more trade than actually happens between India and Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal or Sri Lanka, because nation states have distorted the natural flow. Amit calls this the seen and the unseen at work. The trade we see is small, and the unseen trade that politics prevented would have left people on both sides better off. That makes the region one of the world's great untapped sources of welfare.
core_ideas.quote: the place where the gravity model generates predictions that are vastly above the actual trade is South Asia.

core_ideas.concept: The Expanding Circle — and Why It Isn't Guaranteed
core_ideas.explanation: Lecky's thesis is that moral consideration starts with immediate family and widens to the tribe, the town and the nation, to women, to other races, and eventually to all of humanity. Peter Singer argued it would extend to animals. Amit warns against taking this for granted, since recent decades have brought more polarisation and more 'othering'. Labels like 'foreigner' and 'another country', which quickly becomes 'an evil country', are barriers to the circle widening.
core_ideas.quote: And for me, this expanding circle doesn't give a shit about geography.

core_ideas.concept: Communities of Circumstance vs Communities of Choice
core_ideas.explanation: For most of history, your community was decided for you by geography, caste, class, school and workplace, so you mostly met people like yourself and had little room to grow. The internet lets people form communities around shared interests, values and passions instead. For creators, this means a thousand true fans scattered across the world can sustain the work, and the long tail can thrive as mainstream media and entertainment crumble. Amit says that if he had been born twenty years earlier he would have been a much sadder person, with no audience and no growth.
core_ideas.quote: I could because of technology and the internet, I could move away from communities of circumstance to communities of choice.

core_ideas.concept: The Tyranny of Distance Persists for Atoms and Hugs
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's caution is that distance has died only for electrons. Information moves almost free of cost, but physical goods like pots of honey and sacks of rice are heavy, so borders still matter for them. Human relationships also need physical presence: sharing chai, touching. That keeps the physical movement of people across borders important.
core_ideas.quote: And with physical goods there is no escaping the tyranny of distance.

core_ideas.concept: Borders Can Break a People, If the State Goes All the Way
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay offers a counterpoint to his own argument. Add electrified fences, dogs and machine guns and keep them up for fifty to seventy-five years, and one people can be turned into two. North and South Koreans today can barely talk to each other, and the North has no idea what to make of K-pop. East Germans still carry psychic wounds decades after the Wall fell. Culture is built from daily interaction, and cutting that interaction off for long enough changes it.
core_ideas.quote: That if you will keep the people apart for enough generations, then they will grow apart.

core_ideas.concept: Divided Nations as Natural Experiments in Freedom
core_ideas.explanation: Economics and political science rarely get controlled experiments. Korea and Germany came close: essentially the same people were split in two, and only one half was given freedom. South Korea and West Germany show what free markets and individual liberty can do, while North Korea and East Germany show the tragic alternative.
core_ideas.quote: But in both these cases you had pretty much the same people divided into two and one allowed freedom, the other not allowed freedom

core_ideas.explanation: Walls can also be built with words. Rhetoric and ways of seeing the world can split neighbours living side by side, and Amit sees this happening in India and elsewhere. Ajay asks whether these divisions can override the large gains from trade, friendship and love. Amit answers that the divisions grow sharper under scarcity, missing markets and an oppressive state, because the gains from trade need freedom to flourish.
core_ideas.quote: ways of looking at the world, words, rhetoric, language, can also build those kinds of metaphorical walls between the same people living side by side

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay's opening parable: the Lord holds an accountability session and asks every profession to prove it has added value. The economists include the gravity model on their résumé. The Lord replies, 'Gravity? But that's what the physicists do.' Ajay adds that economists 'all suffer from physics envy, just like me,' and that, 'being imperialists,' they then claimed a general gravity law in the affairs of men.

Ajay suggests that the number of floors between neighbours in a tall building changes how often they meet. Amit replies: 'The secretary of my building is a famous astrologer, apparently. We haven't had anything to do with each other. I don't know which floor he lives on.'

Amit tells Ajay he is 'an economist who has a poet's heart.' Later, after Ajay's line about a border putting 'a line through their heart,' Amit adds: 'In this field right now, there is no border between economists and poets.'
Ajay to Indian nationalists: 'you ain't seen anything yet. If you think of the ferocity, the hatred, the cruelty of nationalism, Europe gets gold medals galore.'
After explaining that fully militarised borders really can split one people into two, Ajay deadpans: 'Not that I'm recommending this to anybody who's watching the show.'
Amit struggling with the director of The Lives of Others: 'Forgive me for the pronunciation. Florian, if you're watching, I'm sorry.'

John le Carré: Ajay says we imagine borders as a one-kilometre demilitarised zone with men holding machine guns, 'like all of us have read in John le Carré novels.' In reality a border is usually just a field.
'Imagined community': Ajay calls the nation an imagined community and says he is 'deliberately playing on the book title.'
Amit interrupts Ajay's point about trade across porous borders to mention 'a song from the film Border about this,' then says, 'Anyway, carry on.'

Ronald Reagan's 'tear down this wall' speech, which Amit sets against Donald Trump's promise to build a wall on the Mexican border: from one Republican president saying 'Tear down this wall' to another who wants to build one.
Joan Robinson's line that whatever you say about India, the opposite is also true. Amit uses it to temper his worry about metaphorical walls in India with some hope.
Paul Graham's 'it's better to be loved by a few than liked by many,' quoted by Amit alongside Kevin Kelly's thousand true fans.

Sport beyond borders: Amit says he cheers for the way Pep Guardiola's teams play, 'from Barcelona to Manchester City,' without any tribal loyalty to those clubs, and for Levon Aronian when he plays chess.
Nabokov is Amit's example of a writer who came to a language late and revelled in it floridly. Agota Kristof did the opposite and stripped her adopted French down to basics.
